title: Sunjata: The Boy Who Could Not Walk

pages.text: In Mali and Guinea, there are families of musicians called griots. A griot plays the kora, a harp with twenty-one strings, and carries in memory the history of kings. The greatest story they tell is eight hundred years old. It begins in the small kingdom of the Mande people, on the upper River Niger. The king had a wife named Sogolon. People mocked her, because she was not beautiful and her back was bent. But hunters who could read the future had told the king: marry this woman, and her son will be the greatest ruler the land has known.
sentences: In Mali and Guinea, there are families of musicians called griots.
A griot plays the kora, a harp with twenty-one strings, and carries in memory the history of kings.
The greatest story they tell is eight hundred years old.
It begins in the small kingdom of the Mande people, on the upper River Niger.
The king had a wife named Sogolon.
People mocked her, because she was not beautiful and her back was bent.
But hunters who could read the future had told the king: marry this woman, and her son will be the greatest ruler the land has known.
pages.alt: A griot seated with a kora, playing before a small audience under a tree.

pages.text: Sogolon had a son and named him Sunjata. He was a strong, healthy baby. But as he grew, something was wrong. At three years old, he could not stand. At five, he still crawled on his hands and knees. At seven, he had the arms of a wrestler and legs that would not hold him. The king’s first wife, Sassouma, laughed loudly. “Is this the great ruler we were promised? My son was walking before he was one.” Sogolon said nothing. She cared for her son, and she waited. Sunjata heard every word, and he waited too.

“Is this the great ruler we were promised?
My son was walking before he was one.” Sogolon said nothing.
She cared for her son, and she waited.
Sunjata heard every word, and he waited too.
pages.alt: A boy with strong arms crawling in a palace courtyard while a richly dressed woman laughs from a doorway.

pages.text: The old king died, and Sassouma’s son was made king in his place. Sogolon and her children were pushed into a small hut at the back of the palace. One day, Sogolon needed baobab leaves for her sauce. She had none, so she went to Sassouma to ask for some. Sassouma held out a basket with a cruel smile. “Take them. My son picked these for me when he was seven. Yours cannot even stand. What use is such a child to his mother?” Sogolon went home weeping, and she told Sunjata what had been said.

pages.alt: A woman with a bent back walking away in tears with a small basket of leaves.

pages.text: Sunjata was silent for a moment. Then he said, “Mother, dry your tears. Today I am going to walk. Send to the blacksmith, and ask for the heaviest iron rod he has. And you shall have baobab leaves: I will bring you the whole tree.” The master smith had been keeping such a rod for years, though he did not know why. Six men carried it to the hut and laid it down. A crowd gathered. Sassouma came to watch and laugh. Sunjata crawled to the rod and took hold of it with both hands.

Send to the blacksmith, and ask for the heaviest iron rod he has.
And you shall have baobab leaves: I will bring you the whole tree.” The master smith had been keeping such a rod for years, though he did not know why.
Six men carried it to the hut and laid it down.
A crowd gathered.
Sassouma came to watch and laugh.
Sunjata crawled to the rod and took hold of it with both hands.
pages.alt: Six men carrying a huge iron rod towards a small hut, with a crowd gathering behind them.

pages.text: He set one end on the ground and began to pull himself up. His arms shook. Sweat ran down his face. His knees left the earth. Slowly, slowly, he rose, and as he rose, the great iron rod bent under his weight, until it was curved like a bow. Then Sunjata let go, and he was standing. The crowd was silent. He took one step, and another. The griot at his side cried out a song that is still sung today. And Sassouma covered her mouth with her hand and went indoors.

The crowd was silent.
He took one step, and another.
The griot at his side cried out a song that is still sung today.
And Sassouma covered her mouth with her hand and went indoors.
pages.alt: A boy standing upright for the first time, gripping an iron rod that has bent into the shape of a bow.

pages.text: Sunjata walked out of the town to a young baobab tree. He put his arms round its trunk, pulled it up by the roots, and carried it on his shoulder to his mother’s door. “Here are your leaves, Mother,” he said. From that day, his strength was known everywhere. He grew up to be a great hunter and leader. Around the year 1235, he defeated a cruel king and founded the empire of Mali, one of the richest that Africa has known. The griots end the story with a warning: never laugh at a child who is slow to rise.

activities.question: Who are the griots?
options: Musicians who keep and tell the history of kings

activities.question: What made Sogolon weep?
options: Sassouma mocked her because her son could not walk

activities.question: What happened to the iron rod as Sunjata stood up?
options: It bent into the shape of a bow

activities.question: Apply it: A classmate is far behind the others in reading, and some pupils laugh at her. Using the legend, what should they remember?
options: A slow start does not decide how far a person will go

activities.prompt: Put the events of the story in order.
items: Hunters foretell that Sogolon’s son will be a great ruler
Sunjata reaches the age of seven without walking
Sassouma insults Sogolon over the baobab leaves
Sunjata stands up with the iron rod
He brings the baobab tree to his mother

activities.definition: A West African musician and storyteller who keeps the history of a people.

glossary.definition: A West African musician and storyteller who keeps the history of a people.
A person who fights by gripping and throwing an opponent.
